system_description.narrative_title: Fragmenting Order: Energy shocks, tech arms race, and regional wars
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, stressed system driven by simultaneous energy-market shocks, renewed great-power competition in technology and space, and multiple region‑level conflicts that propagate through trade, finance and logistics. These dynamics interact: Middle East and Iran‑linked disruptions squeeze oil, diesel and shipping routes, amplifying economic and political pressure; US–China rivalry accelerates militarized AI and space capabilities while sanctions and supply‑chain shifts fragment markets. Multilateral institutions and alliances are being reshaped as states hedge, re-route trade and securitize critical technologies and infrastructure.
system_description.scope: Nation-states and coalitions, global energy and commodity markets, maritime and space domains, advanced-technology ecosystems (AI, semiconductors, cyber), financial sanctions and capital flows, critical infrastructure and logistics chains, and multilateral institutions and diplomacy
system_description.super_system: The planetary political‑economic system: the integrated global economy and interstate order embedded in Earth's geostrategic and ecological constraints
adjacent_subsystems: Maritime trade and critical shipping routes (Red Sea, Hormuz, Suez)
Eurasian security complex (Russia‑Ukraine and neighboring theaters)

variables.name: Middle East energy and maritime insecurity
variables.description: Iran, Houthi proxies, Saudi Arabia and external powers (including the US and regional states) are waging and responding to attacks that are degrading maritime security and constraining oil export routes, producing sustained global supply shocks.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine high‑intensity war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, supported by competing external backers, are escalating drone, missile and aerial-strike campaigns that are changing battlefield dynamics, driving higher defence demand and stressing European security architectures.

variables.name: US–China strategic tech and AI competition
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting leadership in semiconductors, AI and advanced manufacturing through export controls, investment shifts and extraterritorial legal measures, fragmenting supply chains and global technology governance.

variables.name: Orbital weaponization and space arms competition
variables.description: The US, China and Russia are accelerating deployment and doctrinal acceptance of counter‑space and weapons systems in orbit, eroding long‑standing norms and creating a new domain of strategic competition.

variables.name: Western alliance realignment and strain
variables.description: Shifts in US domestic politics, trade disputes and strategic priorities are pushing closer EU–Canada coordination while testing NATO cohesion as allies rebalance defence burdens, trade ties and multilateral cooperation.
